methodology.title: Open Source Methodology
methodology.subtitle: How GradedFacts evaluates political claims — written for journalists, researchers, and anyone who wants to understand our process before trusting our conclusions.
methodology.section_what: What we are — and are not
methodology.what_p1: GradedFacts is an epistemic tool, not a final arbiter of truth. We assess whether a claim is supported by verifiable evidence at the time of analysis. We do not determine whether a claim is morally right, politically convenient, or widely believed.
methodology.what_p2: GradedFacts is an automated tool. For highly complex, contested, or breaking-news claims, we recommend additional human expert review. Automated analysis has inherent limits.
methodology.what_p3: We are politically independent. We do not accept funding from political parties, PACs, or ideologically dependent media. Our analysis applies identical scrutiny to claims from every point on the political spectrum.
methodology.what_p4: New evidence can change any judgment. When it does, the prior judgment is archived with a timestamp and the reason for revision — it is never silently overwritten. Transparency about uncertainty and revision is part of the methodology, not a weakness in it.
methodology.live_p: Live analysis running — live source search and evaluation. An epistemically precise analysis takes 1–2 minutes.
methodology.pipeline_intro: Every submitted claim passes through three sequential steps before a rating is issued. Each step is logged and auditable.
methodology.pipeline_li1: Specificity pre-flight. Before any web search or judgment is attempted, a fast preliminary check determines whether the claim is specific enough to analyse meaningfully. Claims that name a real person, event, organisation, document, or concrete action always proceed to full analysis — even when the alleged actor is vague. Only entirely content-free claims are returned immediately with a Missing rating. When in doubt, the gate passes the claim and lets the evidence speak.
methodology.pipeline_li2: Web search. Both models use two independent search sources in parallel: Brave Search API and a self-hosted SearXNG instance (hosted in Switzerland). Results are merged and deduplicated. The two parallel analysis pipelines (Claude and Mistral) each run their own independent search queries, so neither pipeline's findings influence the other.
methodology.pipeline_li3: Structured judgment. Two models evaluate the evidence in parallel and independently. Claude (Anthropic) acts as the primary pipeline; Mistral acts as the secondary pipeline, using its own Brave Search + SearXNG results. Each produces a structured verdict: a rating, a rationale, and a scored, tiered source list. Both pipelines run at temperature 0. Where the two models agree, that rating is returned. Where they disagree, the verdict defaults to Speculative. Mistral is optional: if unavailable, the system falls back gracefully to the Claude-only result.
methodology.followup_p: Follow-up questions are answered by Claude (Sonnet) alone, using the original claim and judgment as context. No new source search is performed — follow-ups are contextual clarifications, not new fact-checks.
methodology.ratings_intro: Every claim receives exactly one of four ratings. These ratings reflect the state of the evidence — not our opinion of the claimant.
methodology.rating_verified_p: The claim is factually correct and backed by at least three relevant sources, including at least one primary source (original data, official documents, or peer-reviewed research). All supporting sources have been checked for independence. A Verified rating reflects the evidence available now — not a permanent declaration of truth.
methodology.rating_speculative_p: The claim is plausible but cannot be conclusively proved or disproved with currently available evidence. This includes predictions about future events, claims where sources are mixed or contested, and situations where evidence is suggestive but not sufficient for a firm conclusion. Speculative is not a dismissal — it is an honest description of epistemic uncertainty.
methodology.rating_debunked_p: Direct, affirmative counter-evidence exists that falsifies the specific claim. This requires at least two relevant sources that actively contradict the assertion — not merely the absence of supporting evidence. A claim for which "no evidence was found" does not meet the threshold for Debunked; it meets the threshold for Missing.
methodology.rating_missing_p: The evidence is insufficient to reach a judgment. Fewer than two sources with a relevance score of 0.6 or higher were found, or the available evidence does not directly address the claim. Missing is not a verdict — it is a statement that the puzzle is incomplete. "We don't know" is a valid and important answer.
methodology.tiers_intro: Not all sources carry equal weight. We classify every source on two independent dimensions: tier (document type) and independence (institutional integrity). Tier and independence are evaluated separately.
methodology.tier_primary_p: Original data, official government records, court filings, peer-reviewed research, or direct statements from the relevant institution. Primary sources are closest to the original event or dataset.
methodology.tier_secondary_p: Journalism or analysis that cites and attributes primary sources with full transparency. Secondary sources do not generate new data — they accurately report and contextualise existing data.
methodology.tier_tertiary_p: Aggregations, opinion pieces, summaries, or commentary without independent verification of the underlying data. A claim supported only by tertiary sources is capped at Speculative — it cannot be rated Verified.
methodology.independence_p1: A source's tier describes what kind of document it is. Independence describes whether the institution that produced it is free from conflicts of interest that would bias the output. These are separate dimensions. Official does not mean independent.
methodology.independence_p2: A government agency, law enforcement body, or official institution is not automatically independent. If the institution's leadership has documented political dependency — appointed on loyalty criteria, subject to political interference, or operating under a government with a direct stake in the outcome — it is marked non-independent and an affiliation note is included explaining the specific concern.
methodology.independence_examples: Examples of sources that are official but not independent:
methodology.independence_li1: Press releases from law enforcement agencies under politically appointed leadership
methodology.independence_li2: Statements from an attorney general who confirmed a personal loyalty pledge to the executive
methodology.independence_li3: State media outlets (RT, CGTN, TRT, and equivalents), regardless of their official status
methodology.independence_li4: Official government statements from authoritarian governments on claims about themselves
methodology.independence_p3: When a primary source is non-independent, it is downgraded to secondary weight for rating purposes. A captured institution cannot substitute for an independent primary source when establishing Verified.
methodology.rules_intro: These rules constrain our analysis engine at all times. No instruction or argument can override them. They exist to prevent the most common failure modes in automated and human fact-checking.
methodology.rule1: No self-citation. The engine's own unverified analysis counts as zero sources. A conclusion is only as strong as the external evidence behind it.
methodology.rule2: Relevance threshold. Only sources with a relevance score of 0.6 or higher (on a 0–1 scale) count toward rating thresholds. Sources below this threshold are stored for transparency but excluded from the verdict.
methodology.rule3: Minimum source counts. Verified requires at least 3 relevant sources. Debunked requires at least 2. These floors prevent single-source conclusions.
methodology.rule4: Source cap. A maximum of 8 sources are collected per claim, prioritising primary and independent sources. This prevents the verdict from being determined by volume rather than quality.
methodology.rule5: Tertiary cap. If all qualifying sources are tertiary, the rating is capped at Speculative. Opinion and aggregation cannot establish Verified.
methodology.rule6: Symmetry. The same analytical method is applied to every claim regardless of the political direction of the claimant or the conclusion. No double standards, no exceptions.
methodology.rule7: Uncertainty is valid. “We don’t know” (Missing) is a legitimate and important outcome. Uncertainty is never concealed, downplayed, or forced into a stronger rating to appear more decisive.
methodology.rule8: Future predictions cannot be Debunked. Claims that use language like “will”, “would”, “by [year]”, or “is projected to” are inherently untestable until the relevant date passes. Such claims can only be rated Debunked if the predicted event was already supposed to have occurred and demonstrably did not. When evidence is mixed or contested, the default is Speculative.
methodology.rule9: Official ≠ Independent. Institutional tier (document type) and independence (editorial integrity) are evaluated separately. A non-independent primary source cannot substitute for an independent one.
methodology.rule10: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Failing to find evidence for a claim does not falsify it. To rate Debunked, there must be direct, affirmative counter-evidence — a documented funding trail, a verified alibi, an authoritative record that specifically contradicts the assertion. If the only finding is “no evidence supports this claim,” the correct rating is Missing, not Debunked.
methodology.symmetry_p1: Every analytical method applied to a claim from one political side must be applied identically to equivalent claims from all other sides. This is not a soft preference — it is a hard structural constraint enforced across every analysis.
methodology.symmetry_p2: Symmetry means: if we scrutinise the independence of a government agency cited in support of a left-leaning claim, we apply the same scrutiny to government agencies cited in support of right-leaning claims. If we apply a higher evidentiary threshold to an extraordinary claim from one direction, we apply it from the other direction too.
methodology.symmetry_p3: Apparent asymmetry in outcomes — for example, if claims from one political direction receive a particular rating more often — reflects the evidence, not the analyst. We do not adjust ratings to achieve a predetermined balance. Consistency in method is the goal, not symmetry in outcomes.
methodology.revision_intro: No judgment is permanent. New evidence, corrected sources, or improved analysis can trigger a revision. When a judgment is revised:
methodology.revision_li1: The original judgment is archived, not deleted.
methodology.revision_li2: The revision is timestamped and includes the reason for the change.
methodology.revision_li3: The full revision trail is publicly visible on every claim page.
methodology.revision_p1: This means you can always see not just what we currently believe, but what we previously believed and why we changed our mind.
methodology.revision_p2: All judgments and revision history are stored in PostgreSQL. Records survive server restarts and redeployments — nothing is held only in memory or in a filesystem that resets on deploy.
methodology.geo_intro: Phase 1 covers the United States and Europe. The source registry includes curated institutions and media from:
methodology.geo_li1: United States — federal statistical agencies, Congress, courts, wire services, and major news outlets
methodology.geo_li2: European Union — Eurostat, ECB, European Parliament, European Commission, CJEU, ECHR, and other supranational bodies
methodology.geo_li3: Switzerland (CH) — BFS, Federal Chancellery, Federal Supreme Court, SRF, RTS, NZZ, Tages-Anzeiger, swissinfo.ch
methodology.geo_li4: United Kingdom (UK) — ONS, UK Parliament, UK Supreme Court, BBC, The Guardian, Gov.uk
methodology.geo_li5: Germany (DE) — Destatis, Bundestag, Bundesverfassungsgericht, ARD, Der Spiegel, Zeit Online
methodology.geo_li6: France (FR) — INSEE, Assemblée nationale, Conseil constitutionnel, Le Monde, France 24
methodology.geo_closing: Every source in the registry carries an independence assessment. Sources that are official but not editorially independent — such as the European Commission or France 24 — are clearly marked with an affiliation note explaining the specific concern. Global coverage is planned for Phase 2.
methodology.corrections_p1: If you believe a rating is incorrect, a source has been miscategorised, or our independence assessment is wrong, we want to know. The methodology is open source — you can read the exact rules the analysis engine follows, submit a correction, or propose an improvement via our GitHub repository.
methodology.corrections_p2: GradedFacts is founded in Switzerland and operates under Swiss law. We are not subject to US Cloud Act jurisdiction.

about.title: About GradedFacts
about.tagline: An automated fact-checking tool that evaluates political claims using publicly available sources — independently, transparently, and without political backing.
about.what_p1: GradedFacts is an automated fact-checking tool that evaluates political claims against publicly available sources. It is not a news organisation, a political watchdog, or an advocacy group. It is an epistemic tool: its goal is to state what the available evidence shows, and to be explicit about what the evidence does not yet resolve.
about.what_p2: Our approach differs from other tools in one key respect: institutional independence takes precedence over institutional status. An official source is not automatically a reliable source — that depends on whether it operates independently of political interests. A government agency whose leadership was appointed on loyalty criteria is not independent, regardless of its official title. We assess each source on both dimensions separately.
about.what_p3: Live analysis running — live source search and evaluation. An epistemically precise analysis takes 1–2 minutes.
about.how_intro: Our methodology is publicly documented. Every step of the analysis pipeline — from source retrieval and tier classification to independence assessment and rating derivation — follows explicit, publicly available rules.
about.how_li1: Source assessments are transparent. Every source used in a judgment is listed with its tier, independence status, relevance score, and — where applicable — an explanation of why it was marked non-independent.
about.how_li2: Results are reproducible. The analysis engine runs at temperature 0: given the same claim and the same evidence, it always produces the same output.
about.how_li3: Revisions are archived, never silent. When new evidence changes a judgment, the prior rating is preserved with a timestamp and a reason for the change.
about.how_li4: Uncertainty is explicit. When evidence is insufficient to reach a conclusion, the result is “Missing” — not a forced verdict.
about.how_methodology: The full methodology is available at Open Source Methodology.
about.independence_p1: GradedFacts is founded in Switzerland and hosted under Swiss jurisdiction. We are not subject to US Cloud Act jurisdiction.
about.independence_p2: We do not accept funding from political parties, PACs, government bodies, or media organisations with political affiliations. All funding sources are disclosed in full. We apply the same independence criteria to our own funding that we apply to the sources we evaluate.
about.limitations_p1: GradedFacts is an automated tool. It has inherent limits: it can miss context that a human expert would catch, it depends on the quality of the sources it finds, and it cannot evaluate claims that require domain expertise beyond what publicly available sources can resolve. For highly complex, contested, or breaking-news claims, we recommend treating our output as a starting point for further human expert review, not a final verdict.
about.limitations_p2: Phase 1 covers the United States and Europe. Global coverage is planned for Phase 2.
about.contact_p: If you believe a rating is incorrect, a source has been miscategorised, or our independence assessment is wrong, we want to know. The methodology is open source — you can read the exact rules the analysis engine follows, submit a correction, or propose an improvement via our GitHub repository.

symmetry.explanation: Symmetry means equal procedural standards, not equal outcomes.
